fixes.explanation: True. After seven days of camping across from each other, the battle ensues on the seventh day. Israel strikes down the Arameans, a hundred thousand foot soldiers in one day (1 Kings 20:29). You got it, baker.

Double sounds impressive, I'll give it that. But the servants don't say to double anything. They say to raise an army “…like the one you have lost…” horse for horse and chariot for chariot. That's a replacement for what was lost.
This one's easy to flip, so no worries. The text says the opposite. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, approves the plan and acts accordingly (1 Kings 20:25).
That's it. The text says, “…the king approved their plan and acted accordingly.” Ben-hadad is king of Aram, and the plan comes from his servants. He approves it and acts on it.

A small valley is a cozy idea, but the text doesn't put the Arameans there. The Israelites camp like two small flocks of goats, and the Arameans cover the countryside. That's a lot of ground (1 Kings 20:27).

The seashore never comes up in this passage, so no beach day here. The text says the Arameans cover the countryside, while the Israelites are like two small flocks of goats. Two little flocks on one side, and a countryside covered with Arameans on the other (1 Kings 20:27).
An inner room, friend. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, also fled to the city of Aphek and hid in an inner room (1 Kings 20:30). He's hidden away inside the city.
Hurrying back sounds reasonable, but the text doesn't have it. They answer Ahab, “Yes, your brother Ben-hadad.” Then Ahab says, “Go and get him!”

True, and it's a surprise. Ben-hadad, king of Aram, comes out, and Ahab has him come up into his chariot (1 Kings 20:33). A king who was hiding in an inner room is now up in the chariot of Ahab, Israel's king.

A prisoner in Samaria is not what happens. Ahab says to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, “By this treaty I release you…” Then he makes a treaty and sends him away (1 Kings 20:34). So Ben-hadad is released, not kept.

A hood is a classic disguise, and I'd have picked it too. But the text has something different. The prophet disguises himself with a bandage over his eyes while he waits on the road for the king (1 Kings 20:38). Hood didn't get the part this time.
I get the hope for a happy ending. But Ahab says no such thing. He says, “So shall your judgment be; you have pronounced it on yourself.” That's his answer to the prophet's story (1 Kings 20:40).
